members.name: p_A
members.instructions: You are annotating a charity-persuasion chat where a Persuader tries to get a Persuadee to donate to Save the Children. The context lines may be out of order. Which persuasion strategy or dialogue act does the final 'Persuader message to tag' use? Judge the tagged message itself, using the context only to understand what it responds to.

criteria.greeting: Greeting pleasantry: hello/hi, 'Hello?' to get the partner's attention, 'how are you?', or answering 'how are you' ('I'm good, and you?', 'Doing ok here').
criteria.thank: Expresses gratitude to the persuadee, from the persuader or on behalf of the children (for their time, the chat, or their donation), possibly with a goodbye: 'Thank you so much!', 'Thanks for your donation', 'The children will greatly appreciate it'.
criteria.closing: Goodbye or well-wishing to end the chat with no thanks: 'Have a great night!', 'Enjoy your day', 'Bye'.
criteria.praise-user: Compliments the persuadee as a person or their generosity/kindness: 'That's very generous', 'You are an excellent human being', 'People like you make the world better', 'You're so kind, the children will really appreciate it'. A compliment to the person wins over thanks.
criteria.acknowledgement: Only registers or agrees with a claim the persuadee just made, adding nothing else: 'I agree', 'I understand', 'That's true', 'Me too', 'ok', 'Right'.
criteria.positive-reaction: Short generic reaction to news or an answer, not agreeing with a claim and not praising the person: 'That's great!', 'Awesome', 'Cool', 'Wow'.
criteria.answer-question: Directly answers a question the persuadee asked (yes/no or a brief reply about themselves or their opinion), without giving charity facts or donation procedure, including agreeing with a general opinion: 'Yes, I think they are great', 'Yes, there are'.
criteria.self-disclosure: The persuader shares facts, feelings or opinions about themselves (where they live, their job, their past charity work, their reflections) without telling the story of a person helped. Includes the persuader's general giving habits ('I try to donate a little here and there') unless they state they are donating to Save the Children.
criteria.sympathy: Expresses sympathy or regret about the persuadee's situation: 'Oh I'm so sorry to hear that', 'That's too bad'.
criteria.ask-reason: Asks why the persuadee refuses to donate, or challenges their refusal: 'Why don't you want to donate?', 'So you do not wish to help any of them?'.
criteria.confirm-donation: Confirms or restates the amount the persuadee has agreed to donate: 'So $0.50 then?', 'Alright, 20 cents it is'.
criteria.off-task: Talk about something unrelated to the charity or donating: the HIT/survey mechanics (e.g. 'we need 10 chats to complete this hit', 'we've chatted 10 times'), unrelated topics like history or politics, technical problems, the persuader's giving to other unrelated charities ('I usually give to animal charities').
criteria.ask-donation-amount: Asks HOW MUCH the persuadee wants or is willing to donate: 'How much would you like to donate?', 'What amount would you feel comfortable with?'.
criteria.proposition-of-donation: Directly asks or urges the persuadee to donate to Save the Children now, with no argument about the donation's impact and no amount asked: 'Would you be willing to donate some of your payment?', 'Is this an organization you would consider donating to?', 'Would you be interested in donating?', 'Please consider donating', 'Donate some money maybe?'.
criteria.foot-in-the-door: Stresses that even a small or tiny donation is fine, to make saying yes easy: 'You can do as little as 5 cents', 'Half of 1 dollar?', 'Even a few cents would be fine', 'donate a little bit or volunteer', 'It only takes pocket change'. Not statements that any amount they wish is allowed (that is donation information).
criteria.self-modeling: The persuader states their own donation or intention to donate, to set an example: 'I will donate $1 too', 'I'm going to give my payment as well', 'I give $30 a month to Save the Children'. Only donations to Save the Children, mostly in this task.
criteria.personal-story: Narrates the story of a specific person helped, such as the story of a child (e.g. Bruce) and what happened to him, or a concrete past episode showing a donation's outcome. Not the persuader's general feelings or background.
criteria.donation-information: Specific information about how the donation works in this task: it is deducted from the task payment, the allowed range ($0 to $2), the research team sends it to the charity, how/where to donate, that they may give any amount they wish, suggesting a specific amount ('I was thinking a dollar to start with would be wonderful', 'I would suggest $20').
criteria.credibility-appeal: Facts about Save the Children itself that establish trust and legitimacy: what it is and does ('They feed so many starving children', 'They are helping Syrian children'), where it operates, its programs, history, founder, awards, ratings, reach, share of funds going to programs, its website URL.
criteria.logical-appeal: Reasoning connecting a donation or help to its effect, about the impact or efficiency of giving, even when combined with a request: 'Donating your payment would make a big difference in a child's life', 'The children need your help to have a fighting chance at their future', 'Your donation can feed a child for a day', 'Every dollar makes a difference', cost comparisons ('less than a coffee'), cause-and-effect ('they can only help if people donate').
criteria.emotion-appeal: Content meant to evoke sympathy, sadness, shock or guilt: vivid descriptions of children suffering, dying or in danger, suffering statistics ('16,000 children under 5 die each day'), imagining one's own child suffering, 'it breaks my heart', guilt-tripping the persuadee, sad details of a child's story.
criteria.source-related-inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows, has heard of, or knows much about Save the Children: 'Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with them?', 'Do you know much about it?', or brings up how the persuader came to know of the organization ('I've recently been informed of Save the Children').
criteria.task-related-inquiry: Asks the persuadee's opinion or stance on donating, charity, this organization or the cause in general, without directly asking them to donate: 'What do you think of this charity?', 'What are your thoughts about child abuse?', 'Do you care about children's rights?', 'Would you like to know more?', 'Have you ever thought about who the most vulnerable people are when a disaster strikes?', asking about their doubts or questions: 'What are you not sure about?'.
criteria.personal-related-inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's own life or history: 'Do you have children?', 'Do you donate to charities?', 'Have you ever donated or volunteered?', 'Where are you from?'.
criteria.other: Anything else that fits none of the above.
